summary: Semiconductors are in an AI-driven supercycle: third-quarter 2026 global sales were $517.7 billion, up 24.1% on the prior quarter [1], and WSTS implies a 2026 market of about $1,655 billion, up roughly 108% [2]. Guidance from Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and AMD points higher still [3][4][5][6], while the S&P 500 trades at 19.0 times forward earnings [7]. Strength is narrow: memory and AI accelerators dominate, analog is recovering and U.S. solar is cutting guidance [8]. Export controls and AI budget durability are the key risks; we could not source a sector forward multiple.

watch: Whether hyperscaler and AI-lab spending keeps pace with Nvidia's roughly 70% fiscal 2028 growth outlook, which management called supply-constrained [3].
Memory pricing and supply: Micron says 2027 supply is largely committed and tight through fiscal 2028, so any easing would hit margins [4].
U.S. export-control changes for China-bound accelerators, since Nvidia's guidance assumes zero China data center compute revenue [3].
U.S. solar policy, including Section 232 and tax credits, after First Solar cut 2026 sales guidance to $4.6 billion to $4.9 billion [8].
Broadcom's next report, with fiscal Q4 AI semiconductor revenue guided to $21.7 billion [5].

basics.intro: Semiconductor companies design or make the chips that compute, store, move and convert information in almost every electronic device, from AI data centres to cars and phones. Some only design chips and pay others to make them (fabless), some only manufacture for others (foundries), and some do both. GICS also puts solar cell and module makers here, because a solar cell is a semiconductor device. The companies that sell chipmaking machines and materials sit next door, in Semiconductor Materials & Equipment.

products.name: Processors and AI accelerators
products.what: Logic chips that run calculations: CPUs for general computing, GPUs and custom accelerators that run many calculations in parallel to train and serve AI models.
products.examples: Nvidia data-centre GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs, Broadcom custom AI chips

products.name: Memory
products.what: Chips that hold data. DRAM is fast working memory, HBM is DRAM stacked beside an AI accelerator for very high bandwidth, and NAND flash keeps data when the power is off.

products.name: Analog and power chips
products.what: Chips that handle real-world signals such as voltage, sound and temperature, and manage power in everything from factory equipment to cars. Products last for years, so sales are steadier than in logic or memory.
products.examples: Texas Instruments power management and signal-chain chips, Analog Devices

products.name: Networking and connectivity
products.what: Chips that move data: switches and routers inside data centres, network cards, and Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular chips in devices.
products.examples: Broadcom Tomahawk switch chips, Qualcomm modems

products.name: Microcontrollers and embedded chips
products.what: Small, cheap computers-on-a-chip that control cars, appliances, meters and industrial machines.

products.name: Foundry and manufacturing services
products.what: Making chips to other companies' designs. Leading-edge manufacturing is concentrated in very few firms.
products.examples: TSMC (not in the S&P 500), Intel Foundry, GlobalFoundries

products.name: Solar cells and modules
products.what: Semiconductor panels that turn sunlight into electricity, sold to utilities and developers of solar farms.

terms.meaning: A chip company that designs chips but outsources manufacturing to a foundry. It needs far less capital, but depends on the foundry's capacity.
A manufacturer that makes chips designed by other companies.
A company that designs and makes its own chips in its own factories, such as Intel, Texas Instruments or Micron. Its costs are more fixed, so profits swing more with utilisation.
A wafer is the thin silicon disc on which hundreds of chips are made at once. A fab is the factory, which can cost many billions of dollars to build.
The name of a manufacturing generation, such as 3 nm. A newer node packs in more transistors for faster, more efficient chips. The number is now a label rather than a physical measurement.
The share of chips on a wafer that work. Higher yields mean lower cost per chip, which is why new nodes start expensive and get cheaper.
How much of a fab's capacity is running. Because most fab costs are fixed, gross margins rise and fall with it.
Joining several chips, such as a GPU and its HBM stacks, into one package. It is now a bottleneck for AI accelerator supply.
Stacks of DRAM placed right next to a processor so data moves very fast. Every leading AI accelerator uses it, and it sells at a premium to ordinary DRAM.
When a customer chooses a chip for a product it is building. Revenue follows a year or more later, so design wins are a leading indicator.
New orders divided by shipments in a period. Above 1 means orders are running ahead of sales.
How many days of sales a company, or the distributors selling its chips, hold in stock. A rising number often comes before price cuts and a downturn.
Revenue divided by units sold. In memory, ASPs move with supply and demand and drive most of the profit swing.
Government licensing rules that limit selling advanced chips, or the tools to make them, to certain countries, chiefly China.

drivers.name: Data-centre and AI spending
drivers.how: The capital budgets of the big cloud and AI companies set demand for accelerators, networking chips and HBM. When they raise spending plans, orders for these products rise within quarters.

drivers.name: End-market cycles
drivers.how: PCs, smartphones, cars and industrial equipment each have their own cycle. Analog and microcontroller makers depend more on cars and factories; memory makers more on phones, PCs and servers.

drivers.name: The inventory cycle
drivers.how: In shortages customers order more than they need; afterwards they stop ordering while they work the stock down. Chip revenue therefore swings more sharply than demand for the end products.

drivers.name: Memory supply and pricing
drivers.how: Memory is close to a commodity made by a handful of producers (Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron lead). Prices rise when they hold back new capacity and fall when they overbuild, and those prices drive memory makers' profits.

drivers.name: Manufacturing technology and capacity
drivers.how: Leading-edge nodes and advanced packaging capacity decide who can ship the fastest chips and how many. A lead lets a company charge more; a shortfall caps revenue whatever the demand.

drivers.name: Trade policy and subsidies
drivers.how: Export controls can cut off sales to China, tariffs change costs, and subsidies such as the U.S. CHIPS Act pay for new fabs. All of these move revenue and capital spending.

drivers.name: Solar policy and panel prices
drivers.how: For solar makers, tax credits, tariffs on imported panels and global panel prices decide how profitable U.S. production is.

paragraphs: Semiconductors are in the steepest upswing in the industry's history, and it is driven more by an AI capital-spending cycle than by the usual consumer and inventory rhythm. The Semiconductor Industry Association reported on 3 Nov 2026 that third-quarter global sales reached $517.7 billion, up 24.1% from the second quarter, with September sales of $172.6 billion up 146.8% from a year earlier (three-month moving averages compiled by WSTS) [1]. Growth was strongest in the Americas, at 191.7% year on year, but every region was up by more than 70% [1]. WSTS said first-half 2026 sales were $702 billion, up 102%, led by memory (up 305%) and logic (up 45%) [2].

Interest rates and the broader economy matter less than customer budgets here. The wider market is not expensive: FactSet put the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 19.0 on 30 Sep 2026, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and down from 20.4 at the end of June [7]. We think that gap between a cheap-looking index and a surging chip group points to a cycle that is concentrated in AI infrastructure rather than broad. Our read is that the risk is not a macro recession tipping demand over, but a pause in hyperscaler spending, which would hit memory and AI accelerators first. We did not find a sourced reading of central-bank policy rates or currency effects for this brief, so we do not quantify them.

WSTS's spring forecast, as updated in August, implies a 2026 market of about $1,655 billion, roughly 108% growth, and about $2.1 trillion in 2027, roughly 29% growth. WSTS stresses that these are not new forecasts, only the spring scenario with second-quarter actuals substituted [2]. Memory is the swing factor, with 2026 growth of about 302% in that update [2]. These numbers are extraordinary against any history, and we would treat them as a snapshot of a supply-constrained pricing boom as much as a volume boom.

Company commentary supports the structural story. Nvidia reported fiscal Q2 2027 revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106%, with data center at $89.0 billion, and guided Q3 to $108.0 billion plus or minus 2%. Its CFO called a preliminary fiscal 2028 growth outlook of about 70% supply-constrained [3]. Micron said memory and storage supply and demand would be much tighter in fiscal 2027 and 2028 than in fiscal 2026, expected DRAM bit shipments to grow in the low-20% range and NAND in the mid-20% range in calendar 2027 and 2028, and said more than 75% of its 2027 output is already committed [4].

Chips are historically cyclical, and demand is not very price elastic in the short run for AI accelerators but is highly so for consumer devices. AMD's client and gaming revenue fell 8% year on year in Q3 while data center rose 97%, a split that shows how uneven demand is [6]. Long-term demand prospects rest on whether AI customers keep investing; this brief did not find a reliable independent forecast of that spending.

Industry structure differs sharply by segment, so we describe Porter's five forces at the level of AI compute and memory. Rivalry is intense but among few players: Nvidia, AMD and custom-silicon partner Broadcom in accelerators, and a handful of memory makers. Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue was $16.7 billion in the quarter ended 2 Aug 2026, up 221%, and is guided to $21.7 billion next quarter [5]. AMD's data center segment reached $8.5 billion, up 97%, on EPYC and the launch of Instinct MI450 [6].

Barriers to entry are very high: leading-edge design requires large R&D budgets and ecosystems, and manufacturing needs huge capital. Micron's capex plan of about $25 billion in the first half of fiscal 2027 illustrates the scale needed even for one memory maker [4]. Supplier power sits with foundries and equipment makers, which we did not quantify with sourced figures, and Nvidia is working with Micron on a custom HBM4E product, showing how tightly suppliers and customers are tied [4]. Buyer power is concentrated in a few hyperscalers and AI labs; Broadcom's fortunes rest on a small number of such customers, which we infer from its AI revenue scale rather than from a disclosed customer list [5].

Pricing power is currently strong. Micron has agreed most of its calendar 2027 high-bandwidth memory volume with significant price increases [4], and Nvidia guided a gross margin of about 74% [3]. The threat of substitutes is custom chips versus merchant GPUs. Market-share tables by segment were not found in the sources opened.

Regulation is the largest swing factor for the largest companies. On 15 Jan 2026 the Bureau of Industry and Security moved license review for exports of Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X-class chips to China from presumption of denial to case-by-case, subject to conditions: China shipments capped at 50% of volumes for U.S. end use, third-party lab testing, and Know Your Customer rules to prevent unauthorized remote access [11]. Nvidia's August guidance for Q3 assumes zero China data center compute revenue, so any China sales would be upside [3]. We did not find a verified October 2026 export-control update, so this brief does not describe one.

Industrial policy also reshapes the solar-cell and module makers GICS places in this sub-industry. First Solar's CEO called Section 232 action a structural change in how the United States approaches solar manufacturing, and its guidance flags risk from tariffs, export controls, other trade remedies and the Inflation Reduction Act as amended in 2025, including Section 45X credits [8]. The company assumes the current policy environment persists [12].

Technology risk comes from the pace of AI architecture change and custom silicon. Nvidia and AMD ship new accelerator generations on roughly annual cadences, as AMD's MI450 launch shows [6]. First Solar signed a perovskite patent licence, a reminder that solar technology also shifts [12]. We view geopolitical supply disruption, especially around advanced fabrication in Asia, as a standing tail risk but did not find a figure to size it.

Semiconductor economics are unusually strong in this upcycle. Damodaran's January 2026 U.S. dataset, covering 66 semiconductor firms, shows an after-tax operating margin of 34.66% and a return on capital of 41.83%; the 31 equipment firms show 24.24% and 44.88% [9]. Those are industry-wide figures from before the 2026 surge, and company data suggests they have since risen.

Texas Instruments, the analog bellwether, earned a gross margin of about 64.2% and an operating margin of about 47.5% in Q3 2026 (our calculations from its release), on revenue of $6.06 billion, up 28%. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow was $8.4 billion on capex of $2.6 billion [13]. Broadcom generated $13.7 billion of free cash flow on $29.6 billion of revenue, 46% of revenue, with capex of only $0.5 billion [5]. Micron reported an 87% gross margin in fiscal Q4 2026, on revenue of $54.2 billion [4]. Nvidia reported a 75.0% gross margin [3].

Operating leverage is high: AMD's revenue rose 45% to $13.4 billion with non-GAAP gross margin of 56% [6]. Capital intensity differs widely, from fabless Broadcom to memory makers spending about $25 billion in a half-year [4]. First Solar shows the other side: Q3 sales fell 23% year on year, though it still earned about a 57.9% gross margin by our calculation from its release [8]. Margins like these are cyclical peaks in our judgment, not a base case to extrapolate.

Reported results and guidance have been far above prior expectations. Nvidia guided Q3 FY2027 revenue to $108.0 billion against a consensus near $104 billion, with a fiscal Q4 gross margin expected to trough at 71% to 72% on memory costs [3]. Micron guided fiscal Q1 2027 to $61.5 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $38.15, which is the company's own guidance [4]. Broadcom guided fiscal Q4 revenue to about $34.8 billion, up 93% [5]. AMD guided Q4 to about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, implying roughly 66% year-over-year growth at the midpoint [6].

Not everything is rising. TI guided Q4 revenue to $5.80 billion to $6.30 billion and EPS to $2.45 to $2.79, a wide range on a business where its CEO cited broad growth in industrial, automotive and data center [13]. First Solar cut 2026 net sales guidance to $4.6 billion to $4.9 billion from $4.9 billion to $5.2 billion and module volume to 16 to 17 GW [8]. FactSet said Information Technology was one of five sectors expected to post double-digit Q3 earnings growth, but its preview did not give the sector figure [7]. We did not find a consensus 2027 EPS growth number for this sub-industry.

Our view differs from the headline in one respect: the guidance numbers imply that much of the earnings power rests on memory pricing and a few AI customers, so revisions have been upward but are exposed to a change in either.

Valuation is hard to state cleanly because sub-industry forward multiples were not available from the sources we opened. The iShares fund page showed the Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) at a P/E of 42.73 and a price-to-book of 9.13 as of 4 Nov 2026 [10]. BlackRock does not say on that page whether that P/E is trailing or forward, and trailing earnings in a year of rapid growth would overstate the multiple. For context, FactSet put the S&P 500 forward P/E at 19.0 at 30 Sep 2026, versus a 10-year average of 19.1 [7].

A sourced forward P/E for the group and its own history was not available to us, so we avoid stating one. What the reported company numbers do suggest is that expectations are very high. Nvidia is guiding to roughly 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, versus about 44% that analysts had modeled, according to a summary of its call [3], and Micron guided gross margin of 86.25% as its fiscal 2027 low point [4]. A price that capitalizes numbers like these assumes memory pricing and AI budgets stay near current levels.

Our read is that the group is priced for continuation of the cycle rather than for a normal mid-cycle; any normalization of memory margins or a slowdown in customer orders would compress earnings faster than the multiple. Free cash flow yields were not available in the sources opened, though the strong cash conversion at Broadcom and TI is noted above [5][13].

Momentum has been exceptional. BlackRock's page showed the iShares Semiconductor ETF with a year-to-date NAV total return of 50.04% as of 4 Nov 2026, net assets of about $37.6 billion as of 5 Nov 2026, and an expense ratio of 0.33% [10]. We did not find a sourced figure for the S&P 500 over the same period in the pages we opened, so we do not state relative performance. Other secondary reports gave different year-to-date numbers for the chip index, partly reflecting timing and the fund's share split, and we did not rely on them.

Fundamental results support the trend: Q3 sales rose for a third straight quarter by more than 20% sequentially, in the words of SIA's president [1]. Nvidia's shares reportedly fell about 4% after hours following its August results and then reversed to gain more than 4%, a sign of high expectations in the reaction [3].

We did not find short-interest, institutional-flow or breadth data for this sub-industry in the sources opened. Leadership appears narrow, since the group's growth is concentrated in AI compute and memory while analog and solar are mixed, as TI and First Solar results show [13][8].
